narrativeSummary: May 29 closed what may be the most eventful week in markets since the Iran war began, with the S&P 500 posting its seventh consecutive record close and its longest winning streak since 2023, while the Dow crossed 51,000 for the first time. The week's arc was extraordinary: Monday (May 26) reopened after Memorial Day to news of Iran strikes over the long weekend, with the Russell and Nasdaq both rising 1%+ despite them; Tuesday and Wednesday saw the AI enterprise trade ignite with Snowflake +37% and Dell Technologies reporting $43.84B revenue (+88% YoY) with data center growing 181% year-over-year — the most emphatic AI infrastructure earnings print outside of Nvidia all cycle. Thursday brought PCE 3.8% (in-line), GDP Q1 revised down to 1.6%, Iran-US tit-for-tat strikes, and another 'bogus' Iran deal report that nonetheless sent the S&P to record highs as the market priced deal optionality. Friday's session was shaped by White House sources confirming a tentative 60-day ceasefire MOU has been agreed by Iranian negotiators — but Trump wants 'a couple of days to think about it.' Vance told CBS 'we're very close, not there yet.' Iranian state media dismissed the deal reports as 'incorrect.' Oil retreated: WTI at $88-90, Brent at $94-96 — the lowest levels since before the war intensified. The AI narrative ran independently of the Iran drama all week: Dell's data center business grew 181% in a single quarter, the $9.7B Pentagon software deal confirmed government AI spending is accelerating, and Snowflake's $6B AWS commitment cemented the hyperscaler AI demand story. Dell's Thursday AH +38% extended to +29% Friday, making it the second-best day in the stock's history. The month of May closes with the S&P +8%, Nasdaq +8%, Dow +6%, and the 10Y yield falling from its 4.63% 52-week high back to 4.45% as the Iran diplomatic track developed. Real personal income declined 1.1% YoY — the K-shaped consumer story's lower-income stress persists despite the record equity closes above.
macroStressSubtext: 60-day ceasefire MOU tentatively agreed + WTI at $88-90 + 10Y at 4.45% drop MSI 10pts. Deal not final — Trump approval pending. GDP revised to 1.6%, real income -1.1% YoY maintain elevated floor.

The 30Y at approximately 4.96% is back near the 5.00% threshold but below the 5.134% extreme from May 6. The 2Y fell to approximately 3.98% — below 4.00% for the first time since early May, the clearest signal yet that near-term cut expectations are tentatively returning. The 2/10 spread at approximately +45bps is compressing as the long end benefits more from Iran optimism than the short end. H.15 May 28 official confirmed: 10Y 4.45%, 30Y 4.98%, 2Y 3.99%. May 29 H.15 pending 4:15pm. Note: PCE 3.8% in-line (slightly below 3.9% est) and GDP Q1 revised to 1.6% (from 2.0%) were the week's macro data anchors. The revision adds a mild deflationary bias to the growth side — economy growing but slower than initially measured, which slightly improves the Fed cut optionality picture. risks.title: Trump MOU rejection — 'couple of days to think' introduces weekend uncertainty
risks.desc: The most immediate risk: Trump has not yet approved the 60-day MOU. Iranian state media is already calling it 'incorrect.' Trump's history with Iran negotiations includes multiple sudden position changes. If Trump rejects or significantly modifies the MOU, WTI could spike back to $95-100+ on the Monday open. risks.title: Real income -1.1% YoY — lower-income consumer stress is structural and worsening
risks.desc: Real personal income declined 1.1% YoY in April while real PCE rose 2.1% — the K-shaped stress is deepening. Consumers are drawing down savings and credit to maintain spending. American Eagle -11% on comp sales -2% is the retail confirmation. This dynamic — spending above income — is not sustainable beyond 2-3 quarters. If Warsh June 17 holds rates (as expected) and Iran energy costs don't resolve, the lower-income consumer enters a credit stress cycle by Q3.

This delays the energy inflation relief that would most help Warsh's June 17 case for a cut. PCE may not fall below 3.0% until September-October even with an immediate Hormuz reopening. The stagflation trade (short TLT, long TIPS, long energy) has a longer duration than an immediate MOU approval suggests.
